e-7133.problem:
Find a $2 \times 2$ matrix $C$ that has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=1$ and $\lambda_2=-4,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069457/assets/f478b4206f3a8bcc5c025fa0c58bb75430bcb1493c1d8470366864f7fb7ceb6e.png)
e-7133.worked_solution:
Since $\mathcal{B}= \{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $C,$ then $C$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $C=PDP^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $C,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069457/assets/1cf1ba5d93618341227836a110479ebfc258894f9d4f60ae4df1be682d7c74fc.png)

Let ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069457/assets/f1defa7b451fcd56632030e9c3663ad99646c5eabc98eb4e1c5b687687b9fdc4.png) Then

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2} & -\frac{5}{2} \\ -\frac{5}{2} & -\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

e-5502.knowledge_point: Raising a Matrix to a Large Power Using the Properties of Diagonalization
e-5502.worked_solution:
First,  notice that

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069457/assets/9c5de663d2cf109c4faaf839760b0afac6dcbf5ab533570100167727853cb74f.png)

So, we have been given the following diagonalization of $A\mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069457/assets/3f73ff47f00cf345f0ac0cffd41dc325faf00c9f1d1c0ffe4ad7228e83fef3fa.png)

Since $A=PDP^{-1},$ we can compute $A^k$ by using the formula 

$$
A^{k} = PD^{k}P^{-1}.
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{100} & =P{D}^{100}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{100}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{1}^{100} & 0 \\ 0 & {0}^{100}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Restoring a Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
content.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $F$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -4\end{aligned}]
$$
content.worked_solution:
Since $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $F,$ then $F$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $F=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $F,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
F={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}].$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -10 \\ 4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-26 & -30 \\ 24 & 28\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Since $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $S,$ then $S$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $S=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $S,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
S={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}].$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}18 & 1 \\ 15 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}13 & -12 \\ 10 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $S$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Since $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $S,$ then $S$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $S=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $S,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
S={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}].$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}18 & 1 \\ 15 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}13 & -12 \\ 10 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Restoring a Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
content.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=5,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Since $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $A$, then  $A$ must be diagonalizable. 

So, we can write $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $A$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
A={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain,

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 15 \\ 4 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $C$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=10$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=5,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
Since $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $C,$ then $C$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $C=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $C,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
C={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}10 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}](-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}10 & 15 \\ 20 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -2 & 11\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write $C=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $C,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
C={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}10 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}](-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}10 & 15 \\ 20 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -2 & 11\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We have been given the following diagonalization of $A.$

$$
A={{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $A=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${A}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{A}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]=-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{97} & =P{D}^{97}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{97}{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}(-1)^{97} & 0 \\ 0 & {1}^{97}\end{aligned}](-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
We have been given the following diagonalization of $A.$

$$
A={{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $A=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${A}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{A}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]=-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{97} & =P{D}^{97}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{97}{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}(-1)^{97} & 0 \\ 0 & {1}^{97}\end{aligned}](-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since A=PDP^{-1}, A^{69}=PD^{69}P^{-1}. Because 69 is odd, D^{69}=diag(1,-1). With P^{-1}=[[-1/2,-1/6],[0,-1/6]], multiplication gives A^{69}=[[1,2/3],[0,-1]], option b.

after.name: Question 7
after.worked_solution:
We have been given the following diagonalization of $A.$

$$
A={{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $A=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${A}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{A}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}-6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{69} & =P{D}^{69}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{69}{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{1}^{69} & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^{69}\end{aligned}](\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}-6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{2}{3} \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
First, notice that

$$
{[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have been given the following diagonalization of $C:$

$$
C={{[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt[18]{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[36]{3}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Since $C=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${C}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{C}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{36} & =P{D}^{36}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt[18]{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[36]{3}\end{aligned}]}^{36}(\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}(\sqrt[18]{3})^{36} & 0 \\ 0 & (\sqrt[36]{3})^{36}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{3}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & {3}^{1}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}27 & -3 \\ -27 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}15 & 6 \\ -12 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that

$$
{[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have been given the following diagonalization of $C:$

$$
C={{[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt[18]{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[36]{3}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Since $C=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${C}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{C}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{36} & =P{D}^{36}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt[18]{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[36]{3}\end{aligned}]}^{36}(\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}(\sqrt[18]{3})^{36} & 0 \\ 0 & (\sqrt[36]{3})^{36}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{3}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & {3}^{1}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}27 & -3 \\ -27 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}15 & 6 \\ -12 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
